pitch_detail.notes: Warm-up. The start is a two-bolt anchor on a short vertical wall in the middle of the granite apron. Wander up the easy slab a few metres right of Africa Flake until the angle steepens; gear placements plus a single bolt lead to the anchor.
First real friction: four bolts protect moves on small knobs, then one gear placement and a last bolt reach the anchor. Pure smearing and edging on sticky knobbed granite.

Follow a left-facing edge for about 10 m to a bolt guarding a diagonal dike crossing. Good knobs and four bolts lead across a rock bridge around a hole in the slab; one more bolt and some gear finish at the anchor.
Easy knobby ground past four bolts to a ledge on top of the feature to the right. There is no need to climb on the dirty feature itself.
The first bolt protects moves over a sill, then four more lead through big breadloaf knobs. Aim for a clean crack above, protect it with gear and follow it to the anchor.

Bolts protect the entry into a thin crack, very narrow at the bottom and widening as it rises; bring tiny nuts and cams (1/8 to 1/2 inch). From the top of the crack, two bolts lead left over a pair of overlaps; above the second overlap, go straight up a path through the bushes to the anchor.

Move the belay first: walk through the Bubba Compactor (a ledge behind a big detached flake), step down and contour to a thin ledge with a belay bolt, backed up with a 2-inch piece. Clip a bolt, protect the big flakes with gear, then two bolts on top of the flake guard the crux step up a thin dike. Four bolts on the slab above reach the anchor.
Six bolts of thin, sustained friction slab lead to a hole in the rock that takes gear from 1 to 3 inches for the belay.

Step right past a bush to find the first bolt. Smear up and across a right-facing edge, trend right along bolts, then continue up thin ground past more bolts. A 1-inch piece in an overlap crack leads to the anchor.

The most delicate slab: smearing on small knobs past eight bolts to a horizontal crack that takes a 2-inch cam, then two more bolts to a left-facing corner with a gear placement. The anchor sits on top of a pedestal.

Climb past a couple of right-facing corners on gear and clip two bolts to reach the Inverted Prow dihedral, which takes only very small cams. Follow the ramp beside it, then move up onto the buttress crest to a chain anchor.
Blocky, ledgy climbing up the right side of the buttress crest to an anchor on the crest.
Scramble up the ridge until trees force a move right. Step down onto the slab layer just under the trees and follow its dihedral, which protects well, to an anchor on a small stance.

Step right past a clean 3-inch crack and around the bulge up and right. Climb a rib with a horizontal crack that takes a 1/2-inch piece, then a bolt; past bushes, a white rib has one more bolt. Go left of a tree with an old sling and through wide cracks between blocks to the summit chain anchor.

P1 regraded 5.6-5.7 → 5.5, P11 5.7-5.8 → 5.7 (range grades replaced by the FA topo's single grade). Bolt counts are only where the description enumerates every bolt on that pitch (P1,2,3,4,5,7,8,10,11,14); left out on P6/P9 ('a couple', ambiguous enumeration) and P12/P13 (none mentioned). Anchor only on P11/P14 (source says 'chain anchor' for those two); no lengths (none given). Dropped stored claims not found in the source: 'Middle C' section name, 'one key bolt' on P11 (source: two bolts), tree anchors and rope drag on P13-14. Single primary source (FA party's own description) → medium.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.8; the FA description grades it 5.8+. Stored climbing descent note says parties rappel to 'the Pitch 13 chain anchor' — the source names chain anchors at the tops of P11 and P14; P13's anchor type is not stated. Stored beta's 'Middle C' name and 'roughly pitches 7-10' could not be confirmed. The start is a two-bolt anchor on a short wall mid-apron, reached by scrambling down 20-30 m of ramps from the grassy saddle (useful for the approach column).

pitch_detail.notes: Find the narrow whale's-back rib between two facing corners; the nine bolts are hard to see in the shade. A bouldery 5.9 move gains the rib, then 5.7-5.8 friction leads to polished rock near the top with a few more 5.9 moves. Step onto a flake on the left, place gear in good cracks just above, then traverse right to the belay ledge.

The character of most of the route: friction on brilliant white granite covered in knobs and bumps, mostly 5.4-5.6. Bolts are spaced roughly 10-20 feet apart and hard to spot in shade, so look ahead before leaving each anchor.
More knobbed slab at 5.6 with occasional 5.8 moves. On rappel, 60 m ropes let these two pitches be combined into one rappel.
A 5.8 section starts on this pitch, and it can carry running water even when the rest of the route is dry. Be ready for wet smears on this pitch.
There is a gear crack on this pitch that is easy to miss; climbing past it turns the pitch into a long runout. Look for it before running it out.

Climb up and right past four bolts (nothing harder than 5.7), then finish on clean 5.7 splitter cracks and a few face moves past the left side of an overhang, onto the forested ledge on top of the buttress with views of Whitehorse Mountain. The wall's true summit is further up brushy scrambling.

review.changed: 5 → 6 entries. P1 and P12 rewritten with full sequence and bolt counts (9 and 4, both stated). Added P9 (easy-to-miss gear crack). Range grades removed from 2-4, 5-6 (not single tokens; ranges moved into notes) and the stored '5.6' removed from P7 because a source puts a 5.8 section starting on P7 — no source gives a single grade for those rows. No lengths (source only says most pitches take a full 50 m). P8, P10, P11 have no pitch-level description anywhere found. Web research was cut off by a tool limit before the FA trip report on CascadeClimbers could be read; that TR likely has full pitch detail and should be read on a later pass.
review.other_findings: Stored P7 grade 5.6 conflicts with a report placing a 5.8 section at the start of P7. Mountain Project gives the approach as about 3 hours to the start; the stored approach says the basin is ~2 hours from the car. The route tops out on a forested ledge; reaching the wall's summit involves further brushy scrambling (a trip report also describes two sparsely protected leads and a 30 m directional rappel on that exit).
